questions.prompt: A circle has differentiable radius r(t) and area A(t)=π[r(t)]², with time t in seconds. Which equation relates their time rates?
questions.explanation: Differentiate the relation with respect to the common independent variable t. The chain rule gives A′(t)=π·2r(t)·r′(t), or dA/dt=2πr(dr/dt). The factor dr/dt connects the geometric radius derivative to a time rate. A: The square’s derivative is multiplied by the radius time-rate. B: This is dA/dr and omits the conversion from radius change to time change. C: The derivative of a square is not the square of the derivative. D: This omits the current radius factor.

questions.prompt: A sphere’s volume is V=(4/3)πr³. At an instant r=2 cm and dr/dt=3 cm/s. What is dV/dt then?
questions.explanation: Differentiate before substituting the instantaneous radius: dV/dt=4πr²(dr/dt). Now use r=2 and dr/dt=3 to obtain 4π(2²)(3)=48π cm³/s. Radius is changing, so its current value is not a constant radius for differentiation. A: This omits the radius time-rate 3. B: The derivative 4πr²(dr/dt) gives 4π·4·3. C: This uses r rather than r² in the derivative. D: The positive radius rate makes the volume rate positive.

questions.prompt: A rectangle’s length L(t) and width W(t) both vary differentiably with time. Which relation follows from A(t)=L(t)W(t)?
questions.explanation: Differentiate both changing factors with respect to t: A′=L′W+LW′. The length rate sweeps out area across the current width, while the width rate sweeps out area across the current length. A: A product derivative is not the product of derivatives. B: The current opposite side lengths must weight the two contributions. C: Each side contributes a weighted area rate through the product rule. D: This weights each changing side by itself rather than the opposite side.

questions.prompt: At an instant a rectangle has length 5 cm and width 3 cm. Length increases at 2 cm/min while width decreases at 1 cm/min. What is the area time-rate?
questions.explanation: The width’s derivative is −1 cm/min. The product rule gives A′=WL′+LW′=3·2+5(−1)=6−5=1 cm²/min. The two contributions nearly cancel, but the area is still increasing. A: This treats the decreasing width rate as positive. B: This multiplies the two side rates and omits the current side lengths. C: This uses only the magnitude of the shrinking-width contribution. D: Use 3(2)+5(−1)=1, with a negative width rate.

questions.prompt: Differentiable lengths x(t) and y(t) satisfy x²+y²=100. At an instant x=6 m, y=8 m and dx/dt=2 m/s. What is dy/dt?
questions.explanation: Differentiate the persistent relation with respect to t: 2x x′+2y y′=0. Then y′=−(x/y)x′=−(6/8)·2=−3/2 m/s. The stated lengths satisfy 36+64=100. A: The common-time derivative gives x x′+y y′=0, so y′=−6·2/8. B: This omits the negative sign required by the fixed sum of squares. C: This reverses the x/y factor. D: A constant sum of squares does not require each changing length to be constant.

questions.prompt: A cone has volume V(t)=(π/3)[r(t)]²h(t), and both radius and height vary differentiably. Which time-rate equation is correct?
questions.explanation: Keep both varying dimensions as functions of time. Applying the product rule to r²h gives (2rr′)h+r²h′. The constant π/3 remains a multiplier, giving the selected equation. A: This drops the current height and squared-radius weights. B: The product rule handles r²h and the chain rule differentiates r². C: This multiplies rates instead of adding the two product contributions. D: This changes a constant coefficient but does not differentiate either varying dimension.

questions.prompt: A cylinder has fixed radius 3 cm and volume V(t)=πr²h(t). Water volume increases at 18π cm³/s. What is dh/dt?
questions.explanation: Because radius is fixed throughout the process, V=9πh and V′=9πh′. Solving for the height rate gives h′=18π/(9π)=2 cm/s. Here treating the radius as constant is justified by the stated persistent condition. A: This omits the base-area factor 9π. B: This uses radius 3 rather than its square in the base area. C: For fixed r, V′=9πh′, so 18π/(9π)=2. D: Increasing volume in a fixed-radius cylinder requires increasing height.

questions.prompt: A cylinder has varying radius r(t) and height h(t), with V(t)=πr(t)²h(t). At one instant h=5. Why is replacing h by 5 before differentiating not generally justified?
options: Numerical values can never be substituted into a derivative equation.
The cylinder volume formula is invalid when its height is 5.
Differentiating h=5 at one instant proves h′=0 there.
An instantaneous height value does not imply h′=0; substituting first can erase the term πr²h′.
questions.explanation: The correct equation is V′=2πrh r′+πr²h′. The value h=5 may then be inserted at the stated instant, but h′ remains unless a persistent fixed-height condition or a zero height rate is given. Substituting a point value too early can delete a real rate contribution. A: They may be substituted after the correct variable-rate relation is established. B: The geometric formula remains valid; the issue is the time dependence of height. C: A point equality alone cannot be differentiated as an interval identity. D: A value known at only one instant is not a constant relation throughout a time interval.

questions.prompt: A cone keeps the geometric relation r(t)=h(t)/2 as it changes. Its volume is V=(π/3)r²h. Which relation correctly eliminates r and gives the volume time-rate?
questions.explanation: The relation r=h/2 holds throughout the process, so r²=h²/4 can be substituted before differentiation. Then V=(π/3)(h²/4)h=πh³/12. Differentiating with respect to time gives V′=(πh²/4)h′. A: Substitute the persistent similarity relation, then apply the chain rule. B: This fails to square the factor 1/2 in r². C: This omits the height time-rate from the chain rule. D: The derivative of a cube is not the cube of its derivative.

questions.prompt: A student knows dV/dr=4πr² for a sphere and needs dV/dt while the radius changes with time. Which additional step is required?
options: Replace dV/dt directly by 4πr² without any other information.
Multiply 4πr² by dr/dt so both sides describe change with respect to time.
Divide 4πr² by dr/dt in every case.
Square dr/dt because the radius appears squared in 4πr².
questions.explanation: For V(r(t)), the chain rule is dV/dt=(dV/dr)(dr/dt)=4πr²(dr/dt). The quantities must be differentiated with respect to the correct common independent variable; a radius derivative alone is not a time derivative. A: That expression has area units rather than volume-per-time units. B: The chain rule connects a volume-per-radius rate to a radius-per-time rate. C: The chain-rule factors multiply, not divide. D: The radius power is already accounted for by dV/dr; its time-rate is an additional first-power factor.

questions.prompt: Dimensionless sensor variables satisfy y(t)=1/x(t). At an instant x=2 and dx/dt=−3 per second. What is dy/dt?
questions.explanation: Differentiate the relation with respect to time: y′=−x⁻²x′. At the stated instant this gives −(1/2²)(−3)=3/4 per second. The reciprocal variable is increasing as the positive x value decreases. A: This loses the reciprocal derivative’s negative sign. B: This uses x rather than x² in the denominator. C: The derivative is −x⁻²x′, so −(1/4)(−3)=3/4. D: Knowing a current x value does not make x constant in time.
